\section[comprobar]{comprobar — to check, to verify}

\label{lesson:ES-C587-comprobar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the pretext, then the Spanish for to show.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: comprobar}
\textbf{comprobar} — \textquotedblleft{}to check, to verify\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Comprueba el precio antes de pagar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Check the price before paying.}
\end{quote}

Stem change o$\to$ue: \emph{compruebo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{comprobar} is inherited from Latin \emph{comprobare} 'to confirm, to approve', built on \emph{probare} 'to test' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{comprobar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{comprobar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the pretext, then the Spanish for to show, then say \emph{comprobar} again
\end{itemize}

\section[evidente]{evidente — evident, obvious}

\label{lesson:ES-C587-evidente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to show, then the Spanish for to check.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: evidente}
\textbf{evidente} — \textquotedblleft{}evident, obvious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es evidente que está cansado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is obvious that he is tired.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Es evidente que} + indicative.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{evidente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{evidens} 'clearly visible', built from \emph{ex} and \emph{videre} 'to see' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{evidente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{evidente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to show, then the Spanish for to check, then say \emph{evidente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does evidente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Evident, obvious\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[obvio]{obvio — obvious}

\label{lesson:ES-C587-obvio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to check, then the Spanish for evident.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: obvio}
\textbf{obvio} — \textquotedblleft{}obvious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La respuesta es obvia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The answer is obvious.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Es obvio que} + indicative.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{obvio} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{obvius} 'standing in the way', built from \emph{ob} and \emph{via} 'road': the obvious is what you meet on the road (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la certeza]{la certeza — the certainty}

\label{lesson:ES-C587-certeza}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for evident, then the Spanish for obvious.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la certeza}
\textbf{la certeza} — \textquotedblleft{}the certainty\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No tengo la certeza.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am not certain.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Con certeza} — for sure.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{certeza} is built on \emph{cierto} with the ending \emph{-eza}; \emph{cierto} is inherited from Latin \emph{certus} 'settled, sure' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for evident, then the Spanish for obvious, then say \emph{la certeza} again

\section[aparentemente]{aparentemente — apparently}

\label{lesson:ES-C587-aparentemente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for obvious, then the Spanish for the certainty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aparentemente}
\textbf{aparentemente} — \textquotedblleft{}apparently\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aparentemente, todo va bien.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Apparently, everything is going well.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Aparente} + \emph{-mente}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aparentemente} is built on \emph{aparente} and \emph{-mente}; \emph{aparente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{apparens}, from \emph{apparere} 'to appear' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aparentemente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aparentemente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{aparentemente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for obvious, then the Spanish for the certainty, then say \emph{aparentemente} again
\end{itemize}
